Dogface
DAWG-fays
noun (Silent Generation slang)
US Army slang for an infantry soldier, recorded by the early 1940s and of uncertain origin. Soldiers used it of themselves, with a mixture of grumbling and pride, for the foot soldier who walked, dug, and endured; it was common in wartime newspapers and cartoons and in the memoirs of the men who served.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1944 a dogface was a foot soldier — the GI who walked where the trucks could not go, dug his own hole, slept in the mud, and ate cold rations. The men called themselves dogfaces with a grumble and a grin. It was not a proud title, and that was the point: the infantryman knew he did the hardest, plainest work of the war and got the least credit for it. Scripture honours that kind of man. Paul used him as a picture of the Christian life: "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). When soldiers came to John the Baptist and asked what they should do, he did not tell them to quit; he said, "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages" (Luk 3:14). A Roman centurion understood faith better than anyone in Israel because he understood orders: "I am a man under authority" (Mat 8:9). The dogface was looked down on, and there is One who knows that better than any soldier. Christ was "despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isa 53:3). He took the lowest place on purpose, and He said, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13). Then He did it. Many a dogface did the same for the man in the next hole. When your grandfather or great-grandfather says he was just a dogface, thank him — and thank the Lord who honours the lowly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (WWII Army) for the infantryman, the plain foot soldier — a lowly name for hard, faithful service, which Scripture honours in the good soldier who endures hardness (2Ti 2:3).

expand to see more

DOGFACE, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; US Army) An infantry soldier; a foot soldier, used by the men of themselves. "We were just dogfaces — we walked the whole way."

Decode for families: a dogface was a foot soldier — the man who did the hardest work and asked for the least credit.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:3 — "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ."

Luk 3:14 — "And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages."

Mat 8:9 — "For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it."

Isa 53:3 — "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not."

Joh 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

Modern Corruption

A self-deprecating soldiers’ word, not a sinful one; the only care is to use it with the respect the men who earned it deserve.

expand to see more

The infantrymen who called themselves dogfaces were not running themselves down so much as telling the truth about hard service with a soldier’s humor. There is nothing in the word to condemn, and much in the men to honour.

The care belongs to those who were not there. A word a soldier uses of himself is not a word for others to use in contempt. Grandchildren who hear it should hear it as Scripture would have them hear it: as the name of a man who endured hardness (2Ti 2:3) and, often enough, laid his life on the line for his friends (Joh 15:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English dog + face → early 1940s US Army slang (the infantryman, used of themselves) → WWII newspapers, cartoons, and memoirs → a veterans’ word.

expand to see more

English dog — long used in slang for a lowly, hard-used fellow

Early 1940s US Army: dogface — an infantry soldier; origin uncertain

1940s: soldiers’ self-name, common in wartime papers and cartoons

Postwar: a veterans’ word for the foot soldier
